extracted.intended_audience: employers, human resources professionals, labor/employment attorneys, and stakeholders participating in DOL rulemaking on the FLSA EAP exemption
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final-rule rationale for revising the FLSA part 541 earnings thresholds (standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation), establishing methodologies for setting them, and creating a triennial updating mechanism and effective/applicability dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department authority to adopt a salary level test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary's authority under section 13(a)(1) to 'define[]' and 'delimit[]' the terms 'bona fide executive, administrative, or professional capacity' includes the authority to use a salary level test as one criterion for identifying EAP employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department relies on longstanding practice (salary test in part 541 since 1938), judicial precedent (including Mayfield v. U.S. Dept. of Labor), and the fact that Congress has not amended section 13(a)(1) to restrict regulatory compensation requirements. Commenters arguing lack of authority were considered and rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular updating of earnings thresholds to reflect current data
rubrics_metrics.description: Earnings thresholds must be updated periodically so that they remain effective indicators for distinguishing exempt from nonexempt white-collar employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long intervals between updates erode the screening function of salary tests because wages rise over time (historical examples cited). The rule finalizes a mechanism to keep thresholds current rather than leaving them stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial update timing and amounts (July 1, 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial update to the standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation requirement will occur on July 1, 2024 using the methodologies then in place (the 2019 methodologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying current data to the 2019 methodologies results in a standard salary level of $844 per week and an HCE total annual compensation threshold of $132,964. The Department chose the July 1, 2024 initial update to use methodologies familiar to employers and to provide a manageable initial adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date vs. applicability date (staggered implementation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is effective July 1, 2024, but the new standard salary level methodology and the new HCE total annual compensation methodology will not be applicable until January 1, 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department aligned the effective date with the first of a month (and typical employer budget years) for administrability and intentionally delayed applicability of the new methodologies by ~6 months to give employers additional time to evaluate and adjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: New standard salary level methodology (post-applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is setting the standard salary level methodology to the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (currently the South).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodology is intended to 'fully restore the salary level's historic screening function' and to account for the shift to a one-test system in 2004 that otherwise broadened the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: New HCE total annual compensation methodology (post-applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is raising the HCE total annual compensation requirement to the annualized equivalent of the 85th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCE methodology is designed to keep the HCE exemption as a streamlined alternative for employees 'at the very top of [the] economic ladder' and to exclude all but those most likely to meet the duties test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial update schedule (new §541.607)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the initial update, the standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation threshold will be updated every 3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first triennial update will occur three years after the initial update (i.e., July 1, 2027). Subsequent triennial updates will apply the methodologies that are in effect at the time of each update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data window for triennial updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Triennial updates will use current earnings data; specifically, subsequent updates will apply the most recent four quarters of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the most recent four quarters of data ensures the thresholds reflect up-to-date earnings trends at the time of each triennial update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice and pause mechanism for scheduled updates
rubrics_metrics.description: The updating provision includes advance publication of updated thresholds in the Federal Register and a pause mechanism that can delay a scheduled update under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM outlined notice procedures (§541.607(c)) and a pause trigger (§541.607(d)); the Department received comment and added clarifying language regarding the delay provision in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial-update methodology (use of 2019 methodology for initial increase)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial update (July 1, 2024) uses the 2019 rule methodologies: the 20th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time nonhourly workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (and retail nationally) for the standard salary level, and the 80th percentile nationwide for the HCE threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department selected the familiar 2019 methodology for the initial update to limit disruption and because employers are already familiar with that methodology; applying current data to it produced $844/week and $132,964/year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of the initial update and methodological changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial update is intended to be severable from future triennial updates and from the change in methodologies; the initial update will remain in force even if the new methodologies or future updates are stayed or do not take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly states its intent that the initial update remain effective regardless of litigation or stays affecting the later methodological changes or triennial updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of salary level as a screening device in combination with duties tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The salary level must function effectively with the duties tests to help define and delimit the EAP exemption; a salary level that is too low undermines that screening role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasized that the salary level's purpose is to assist in identification of EAP employees based on wages presently received and to prevent the broadening effect of a duties-only approach that shifted the burden onto employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of employer adjustment burdens (effective date length and phase-ins)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department considered commenters' requests for longer effective dates and multi-year phase-ins to mitigate employer burden when implementing increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggested effective dates ranging from 90 to 180 days up to 12–18 months, and various phase-in schedules (e.g., 2–6 years, multi-step increases). The Department weighed these concerns and adopted a July 1, 2024 effective date with delayed applicability of new methodologies to Jan 1, 2025 and a triennial update schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential effective-date considerations for HCE threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering effective dates, the Department treated the HCE compensation threshold differently because relatively few employees earning between the current and proposed HCE thresholds would not meet the duties test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For that reason, the Department believed a shorter effective date was appropriate for the proposed HCE compensation threshold, though it still delayed applicability of the new methodology to align implementation timing with the standard salary methodology.
